summary: Describes how to map between SIP and ISUP, the ISDN User Part of SS7, so that SIP calls can interwork with the public telephone network. It is intended for environments where part of a call goes through the PSTN.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3398 explains how a gateway turns a SIP call setup into the phone network's own signalling, and the phone network's signalling back into a SIP request. It gives the message-by-message flow for a call in each direction, the rules for turning telephone numbers into web-style addresses, and tables that pair each SIP status code with the phone network's reason for ending a call. It also sets out the extra SIP features a gateway needs, such as carrying the phone signalling inside the SIP message so the far end sees the same thing.

subtitle: How a gateway translates calls between SIP and ISUP so internet telephony can reach the phone network and back.

tldr.problem: A SIP phone and a telephone exchange do not speak the same signalling language. SIP sets up sessions over IP, while the phone network uses ISUP, a signalling protocol inside the SS7 system, and a call that has to reach the other side has to be described in both.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the translation in both directions. A SIP INVITE becomes an ISUP Initial Address Message with the five mandatory parameters filled in, and an Initial Address Message becomes an INVITE whose numbers are written as tel URLs. Two parallel state machines keep the two sides in step, and tables say which SIP status code matches which ISDN cause code.
tldr.outcome: A gateway built this way can carry calls between IP and the phone network, and it can carry the ISUP messages themselves inside the SIP message body so that the far end sees the same signalling it would have seen directly. The memo also says what it leaves out: it does not cover the maintenance messages of the phone network, and it warns that embedded ISUP must not be trusted unless the request was strongly authenticated.

today: RFC 3398 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It was written by the IETF Transport Area working groups, and it refers to separate SIP-T documents for the ISUP transparency format, the privacy negotiation and the reliable provisional responses.

sections.title: Two Signalling Protocols and the Box Between Them
sections.content:
SIP is an application layer protocol for establishing, terminating and modifying multimedia sessions, typically carried over IP. A telephone call is a multimedia session in which only audio is exchanged.

The ISDN User Part, ISUP, is a level 4 protocol used in Signaling System No. 7 networks. It typically runs over the Message Transfer Part, though it can also run over IP. ISUP controls telephone calls and the maintenance of the network, for example blocking circuits and resetting circuits.

The module that performs the mapping between the two protocols is usually called a Media Gateway Controller, or MGC, although the terms softswitch and call agent are also sometimes used. An MGC has logical interfaces facing both networks, the one carrying ISUP and the one carrying SIP. It also has some capability for controlling the voice path, and there is typically a Media Gateway, or MG, with E1/T1 trunking interfaces for the voice from the public switched telephone network and with IP interfaces for voice over IP. The MGC and the MG can be merged in one physical box or kept separate.

These controllers are frequently used to bridge SIP and ISUP networks, so that calls originating in the telephone network can reach IP telephone endpoints and the other way round. That is useful when telephone calls need services from the IP world, when IP networks carry telephone-to-telephone calls, and when calls start on a desktop softphone and end at a telephone.

The memo describes the logic and procedures an MGC might use, by showing the correspondences between the two protocols at the message level and the parameter level. It also describes the interplay between the parallel state machines of the two protocols, as a recommendation to implementers on how to synchronize protocol events in an interworking architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP and ISUP are two different ways of saying the same thing to a telephone network. A media gateway controller sits between them, translating in both directions, and usually hands the audio itself to a separate media gateway.

sections.title: Scope and Scenarios
sections.content:
The memo focuses on translating ISUP messages into SIP messages and mapping ISUP parameters into SIP headers. For ISUP calls that traverse a SIP network, the purpose of the translation is to let SIP elements such as proxy servers, which do not typically understand ISUP, make routing decisions based on ISUP criteria such as the called party number. The memo therefore provides a SIP mapping only for the ISUP parameters that intermediaries might use when routing SIP requests. As a side effect, translation also increases interoperability, because it gives SIP endpoints that cannot understand encapsulated ISUP, or that cannot understand the particular ISUP variant it holds, some critical information about the call.

Only the call functionality of ISUP is taken into account. Maintenance messages dealing with telephone network trunks are treated only as far as they affect the control of an ongoing call, and otherwise have neither an analogue in SIP nor need one. The messages indicating error or congestion situations in the telephone network, which belong to MTP-3, and the recovery mechanisms such as the User Part Available and User Part Test ISUP messages, are outside the scope of the document.

There are several flavors of ISUP. The ITU-T international ISUP is used throughout the memo, and the differences with the American National Standards Institute and the Telecommunication Technology Committee versions are also outlined. ITU-T ISUP is used because it is the most widely known of them, and because only a small number of fields map directly from ISUP to SIP, the signalling differences between the ITU-T version and specific national variants generally have little or no impact on the mapping. Local number portability is the exception, since the ITU-T has not substantially standardized practices for it, so it has to be described on a virtually per-nation basis. The number portability practices described in the memo are therefore presented as an optional mechanism.

The mapping of SIP headers to ISUP parameters focuses largely on the Initial Address Message and the INVITE, because both are used to request the establishment of a call. Once an INVITE has been sent, headers such as To and From become essentially fixed, and no further translation is needed during subsequent signalling, which is routed by the Via and Route headers. The memo adds some detail on how the parameters of the Address Complete Message and the Release Message are populated from SIP status codes.

The document describes when the media path of a SIP call is to be initialized, terminated or modified, but not how that is done or with which protocols.

There are several scenarios where ISUP to SIP mapping takes place, and the way the messages are generated depends on the scenario.

In the simplest, a single MGC handles a call between a SIP phone and a telephone, or the other way round, and the MGC generates the ISUP messages by the methods the memo describes. There is one signalling path and no SIP network in between.

The scenario where a call originates in the telephone network, goes into a SIP network and terminates in the telephone network again is known as SIP bridging. SIP bridging should provide ISUP transparency between the telephone switches handling the call, and this is achieved by encapsulating the incoming ISUP messages in the body of the SIP messages. The ISUP messages generated by the egress MGC are then the ones that were present in the SIP body, possibly with modifications. If the called number in the request URI is different from the one in the ISUP, for example because the call was redirected in SIP, the ISUP message has to be adjusted.

SIP is used between the two MGCs because the voice path has to be established through the IP network between the two media gateways. That structure also lets the call take advantage of certain SIP services. The ISUP messages carried in the SIP bodies give the peer MGC further information, such as cause values and optional parameters.

In both scenarios the ingress MGC places the incoming ISUP messages in the SIP body by default. That has security implications, which the memo returns to later. If the recipient of those messages, typically a SIP user agent, does not understand them, a negotiation using the SIP Accept and Require headers takes place and they are not included in the next SIP message exchange.

A signalling gateway may sit between the telephone network and the MGC, encapsulating the ISUP messages over IP. The mapping described in the memo is not affected by the underlying transport protocol of ISUP.

Overlap dialing, which uses the Subsequent Address Message, is outside the scope of the memo. A gateway facing an ISUP network in which overlap dialing is used is expected to implement timers that ensure all the digits have been collected before an INVITE is sent into the SIP network.

Gateways may also receive incomplete ISUP messages, which indicate message segmentation because the message was too long. These are commonly followed by a Segmentation Message carrying the rest of the original message. An incomplete message may not hold enough parameters to map properly to SIP, and encapsulating one may confuse the terminating gateways, so a gateway must wait until a complete ISUP message has been received, which may mean waiting for one or more Segmentation Messages, before sending any corresponding INVITE.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is about calls, not about running the telephone network. It maps the parameters that a SIP proxy would need in order to route a call, and it leaves the network maintenance messages and the details of the media path alone. It then describes the two shapes of interworking: a gateway sitting between a SIP phone and the phone network, and a call that crosses a SIP network with the ISUP messages carried inside the SIP messages.

sections.title: The SIP Mechanisms the Mapping Needs
sections.content:
A correct mapping needs some SIP mechanisms beyond those in the base SIP specification. If the user agent involved does not support them, the call can still go ahead, but its establishment may be slightly different from what the user expects, for example the other party answering before the ringback tone arrives, or the user not being told that the call was forwarded.

Transparent transit of ISUP messages. To let gateways take advantage of the full range of services the telephone network offers when placing calls from the telephone network to itself across a SIP network, SIP messages must be able to carry ISUP payloads from gateway to gateway. User agents that do not understand ISUP are permitted to ignore these optional MIME bodies.

Understanding MIME multipart bodies. In most PSTN interworking situations the SIP message body has to carry session information in the Session Description Protocol as well as ISUP and billing information, so PSTN interworking nodes must understand the MIME type multipart/mixed. Clients express support for it by including multipart/mixed in an Accept header.

Transmission of DTMF information. How the tones a user presses are carried by a gateway is separate from how SIP and ISUP are interworked, but since DTMF carriage is part of a complete gatewaying solution, some guidance is offered: a symbolic method of transmitting the information in band is desirable, and this may be done as described in RFC 2833.

Reliable transmission of provisional responses. Provisional responses, the 1xx class, carry call progress information, and PSTN interworking relies on them for control of the media channel and the timing of call events. When interworking with the telephone network, SIP messages must be sent reliably end to end; reliability of requests is already guaranteed by the base protocol, and one application-layer mechanism for responses is described in a separate document.

Early media. Early media is the capability to play audio before a SIP session has been established, that is, before a 2xx response has been sent. For telephony it is desirable to establish media in the backwards direction so that tones and announcements can be played, especially when interworking with a network that cannot signal call status out of band, such as a legacy multifrequency network. Where interworking has not been encountered, early media is almost always undesirable, because it consumes trunk resources between machines to play media for which no revenue is collected. The baseline SIP protocol has enough support for rudimentary unidirectional early media, since an INVITE almost always contains the SDP needed to send media backwards, but it has limitations: the media streams offered in the SDP of the INVITE cannot be modified or declined, and the bidirectional RTCP needed for session maintenance cannot be established.

Mid-call transactions. There are situations when gateways must send messages to each other over SIP that correspond to no SIP operation. To support mid-call transactions and other ISUP events of that kind, SIP gateways must support the INFO method of RFC 2976, though the memo does not prescribe using INFO to carry DTMF digits. Gateways must accept 405 Method Not Allowed and 501 Not Implemented as non-fatal responses to an INFO request, so that a call in progress is not torn down if the destination rejects it that way.

Privacy protection. ISUP has a concept of presentation restriction, which lets a user say that their number should not be shown to the person they are calling. A gateway receiving an ISUP request that requires presentation restriction must shield the caller's identity in some fashion. The base SIP protocol supports a way of specifying that a user is anonymous, but it has limitations, for example it reveals the identity of the gateway itself, which could be a privacy-impacting disclosure.

CANCEL causes. A CANCEL request cannot carry a message body, so in SIP bridging cases ISUP encapsulation cannot be used to carry the cause code of the Release message end to end. Ordinarily this is not a big problem, because the only reason a Release is issued to cancel a call setup attempt is that a user hangs up while the phone is still ringing, which gives a normal clearing cause. Under exceptional conditions, such as a catastrophic network failure, a Release may be sent with a different cause code, and it would be handy if the SIP network could carry that cause code end to end.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain SIP is not quite enough. The gateway needs to carry the phone signalling inside the SIP message, understand multipart bodies, send the progress messages reliably, be able to play tones before the call is answered, carry mid-call events, respect a request to hide the caller's number, and find a way to pass on a failure reason when a call setup is cancelled.

sections.title: SIP to ISUP: An INVITE Becomes an IAM
sections.content:
When an INVITE arrives at the gateway, a 100 Trying response may be sent back. The hardware resources for the media stream must be reserved at that point, because an IAM cannot be sent before the resource reservation, and especially the selection of the TCIC, has taken place. The resources are typically a time slot in an E1 or T1 and an RTP/UDP port on the IP side. After the IAM has been sent, timer T7 is started, whose default value is between 20 and 30 seconds, and the gateway moves to the Trying state.

The IAM carries five mandatory parameters: the Called Party Number, the Nature of Connection Indicator, the Forward Call Indicators, the Calling Party's Category, and a parameter giving the desired bearer characteristics of the call, which is the Transmission Medium Requirement in some ISUP variants and the User Service Information in others, or both. Every gateway therefore needs a way to fill in each of those five, and most of the values, such as the nature of connection or the user service information, will be the same for every IAM, while the called party number varies from call to call.

Q.763 lists 29 optional IAM parameters, and each of those need not be translated to achieve the goals of the mapping, because the parameters that are only meaningful to the telephone network are carried through a telephone to SIP to telephone network by encapsulation. Only five of them are immediately useful for translation: the Calling Party's Number, the Transit Network Selection, the Carrier Identification Parameter, the Original Called Number, and the Generic Digits, known in some variants as the Generic Address Parameter.

The gateway should make use of any encapsulated ISUP in the INVITE to help formulate the outbound signalling, while also heeding the security considerations. It should reuse the values of the ISUP parameters of the encapsulated IAM where it can, but the relevant values of the SIP header fields must overwrite the values that would have been set from the encapsulated ISUP. The updates to the critical session context parameters created in the SIP network take precedence, which is what lets call forwarding and redirection be implemented in the SIP network. The memo's example: an INVITE arrives carrying an encapsulated IAM whose Called Party Number is +12025332699, but the Request-URI says tel:+15105550110, so the gateway must use the number in the Request-URI. Gateways must be provisioned with default values for the mandatory ISUP parameters that cannot be derived from translation, such as the nature of connection and the transmission medium requirement, and the Forward Call Indicators must have a default too.

The first step of the translation is the inspection of the Request-URI. Where the optional number portability practices are supported, the 'npdi=yes' and 'rn=' parameters of the Request-URI are handled first. Without npdi=yes, the primary telephone number in the tel URL is converted to ISUP format and used as the Called Party Number. With npdi=yes, the Forward Call Indicators bit for number translated must reflect that a number portability dip has been performed. With npdi=yes but no rn=, the main number populates the Called Party Number, which indicates that a portability dip took place but the called party's number was not ported. With both npdi=yes and an rn= field, the ANSI rule is that the rn= number populates the Called Party Number and the main number populates the Generic Digits Parameter, while in other ISUP variants the rn= number is prepended to the main number and the combined result populates the Called Party Number.

For carrier-based routing, a 'cic=' parameter in the Request-URI means the gateway should consult local policy before putting the Carrier Identification Code in the IAM, because with many independent trunks it may need to choose a particular trunk or a tandem for that carrier. Policy should decide whether the Carrier Identification Parameter or the Transit Network Selection carries the code. Without pre-arranged policy, the Transit Network Selection is used when the Called Party Number is in international format, and the Carrier Identification Parameter otherwise where it is supported.

A gateway that receives a Request-URI without a valid telephone number should reject the request with an appropriate response code, but it should keep processing requests whose From header holds no telephone number, as happens when a call starts at a SIP phone that uses the user@host form of SIP URI. In that case the Calling Party's Number parameter should be omitted from the outbound IAM.

When the gateway receives comprehensible encapsulated ISUP, it must set the Forward Call Indicators in the IAM it generates so that all the interworking-related bits have the same values as their counterparts in the encapsulated ISUP, which in most cases say that no interworking was encountered. Without usable encapsulated ISUP, the memo strongly recommends setting the Interworking Indicator to no interworking and the ISDN User Part Indicator to ISUP used all the way, and the gateway may also set the Originating Access indicator to Originating access non-ISDN, because it is not safe to assume that SIP phones support ISDN endpoint services.
sections.plainLanguage: When a SIP request arrives, the gateway reserves the media resources, builds a phone network setup message with the five mandatory parameters, and starts a timer. The number in the request wins over any number that came inside the message body, and the gateway also handles the optional number portability and carrier routing fields.

sections.title: ISUP to SIP: An IAM Becomes an INVITE
sections.content:
When an IAM arrives at a gateway, the gateway should reserve the internal resources needed for the IP side of the call, such as digital signal processors, and may prepare to connect audio in the backwards direction. A SIP INVITE must then be created for transmission into the SIP network.

The context of the call setup request read from the IAM is mapped primarily to two URIs in the INVITE, one representing the originator of the session and the other its destination. The originator always appears in the From header, after conversion from ISUP format, and the destination is almost always used for both the To header and the Request-URI.

Once the address of the called party number has been read from the IAM, it should be translated into a destination tel URL that becomes the Request-URI. Alternatively the gateway may first attempt a Telephone Number Mapping, or ENUM, query to resolve the called party number to a URI. Some additional ISUP fields may be added to the tel URL afterwards. With carrier-based routing, the gateway should look for the Carrier Identification Parameter or the Transit Network Selection, and if a value is present the Carrier Identification Code should be extracted, analysed by the gateway and appended as a 'cic=' field if local policy allows. With number portability-based routing, an 'npdi=yes' field should be appended to record that a portability dip has been performed, and where a Generic Address Parameter is present, its contents should be translated and copied into an 'rn=' field while the Generic Address Parameter itself is translated and used for the primary telephone number of the tel URL. Since location routing numbers are necessarily national in scope, they must not be preceded by a '+' in the 'rn=' field.

In most cases the destination tel URL is used in both the To field and the Request-URI. If the Original Called Number parameter is present in the IAM, however, the To field should be built from the translation of that parameter, and the Request-URI and the To field may then differ.

The From header depends on the presence of the Calling Party's Number parameter. If it is not there, the gateway should create a From header holding a SIP URI without a user portion, which communicates only the hostname of the gateway. If it is there, it should be translated into a tel URL for the From header. In either case local policy, or a request for presentation restriction, may produce a different value.

The responses coming back are mapped in the same way. A 100 response should not trigger any PSTN interworking messages; it only serves to suppress INVITE retransmissions. When an 18x provisional response arrives and no ACM has been sent and there is no legitimate ISUP in the body, the message to send is chosen from a table: 180 Ringing produces an ACM with the Backward Call Indicators set to subscriber free, 181 Call is being forwarded produces an early ACM and a CPG with event 6, and 182 Queued and 183 Session progress each produce an ACM with the Backward Call Indicators set to no indication. If an ACM has already been sent, the same responses produce CPG messages instead: event 1 Alerting for 180, event 6 Forwarding for 181, and event 2 Progress for both 182 and 183.

When they receive an ACM, switches in many ISUP networks start a timer known as T9, which usually lasts between 90 seconds and 3 minutes. While early media is being played, that timer lets the caller hear backwards media from the remote switch, in the form of ringback, tones or announcements, without being charged for the connection. Some networks do not support timer T9.

On a 200 OK the gateway must establish a directional media path and send an ANM to the telephone network as well as an ACK to the SIP network. If the 200 OK arrives before the gateway has sent an ACM, a CON is sent instead of the ANM in the ISUP variants that support the CON message.

A 3xx response, which is a redirection, should be handled by sending new call setup requests using the URIs in any Contact header fields, as the base SIP specification requires. If a particular URI is best reachable through the telephone network, the gateway should send a new IAM and from that moment act as an ordinary telephone switch with no SIP involved. Alternatively the gateway may send a Release message to the telephone network with a redirection indicator of 23 and a diagnostic field for the number in the URI. While it is exploring a long list of Contact header fields, the gateway may send a CPG with event code 6, Forwarding, to show that the call is proceeding. All redirection situations have to be treated carefully because they involve special charging: in the telephone network the caller typically pays for the first leg to the gateway and the callee pays for the second, from the forwarding switch to the destination.
sections.plainLanguage: When a setup message arrives from the phone network, the gateway turns it into a SIP request. The called number becomes the destination address, the calling number becomes the From header, and each SIP response is turned back into the phone network's own progress or answer message.

sections.title: Cause Codes and Status Codes
sections.content:
The Release message in the SS7 network is used in a very general way, while SIP has several specific tools that together play the same role: BYE, CANCEL and the status codes. A Release can tear down a call already in progress, which is a BYE; cancel a call setup request that has not completed, which is a CANCEL; or reject a setup request that has just arrived, which is a status code.

Some ISDN cause codes should not be mapped at all, because they are only meaningful to the ISUP interface of a gateway. The example the memo gives is cause code 44, request circuit or channel not available: it means the circuit the setup was sent on was thought to be in a state incompatible with a new call, and the right response is for the originating switch to send the setup again for a different circuit, not to tear the call down. There is no SIP status code for choosing a new circuit, so receipt of cause code 44 should not produce any SIP status code at all. If a cause value other than those listed is received, the default response of 500 Server internal error should be used.

The Cause and Location parameter also carries a cause location that says which entity was responsible for ending the call, the most important distinction being between the user and the network. In most cases the location does not affect the mapping, and a diagnostic field may also be present with extra data about how the call ended. The memo then gives the recommended mappings, grouped by kind: normal events, where for example 1 unallocated number, 2 no route to network and 3 no route to destination all become 404, 16 normal call clearing usually results in a BYE or CANCEL, 17 user busy becomes 486 Busy here, 18 no user responding becomes 408 Request Timeout, 21 call rejected becomes 403 Forbidden, and 27 destination out of order becomes 502 Bad Gateway; resource unavailable, where 34, 38, 41, 42 and 47 all become 503 Service unavailable; service or option not available, where 55 and 57 become 403 and 58 becomes 503, and 65, 70 and 79 become 488 or 501; invalid message, where 87 becomes 403 and 88 becomes 503; protocol error, where 102 becomes 504 Gateway timeout and 111 becomes 500; and interworking, where 127 becomes 500.

The other direction works the same way. When a Release is generated because of a SIP rejection, the Cause and Location parameter should be set to the value carried in an encapsulated Release if there is one. Otherwise the recommended mapping sends 400 Bad Request to cause 41 Temporary Failure, 401 Unauthorized and 407 Proxy authentication required to 21 Call rejected, 404 Not found to 1 Unallocated number, 405 Method not allowed to 63 Service or option unavailable, 408 Request timeout to 102 Recovery on timer expiry, 410 Gone to 22 Number changed, 480 Temporarily unavailable to 18 No user responding, 482 Loop Detected and 483 Too many hops to 25 Exchange, routing error, 484 Address incomplete to 28 Invalid Number Format, 486 Busy here and 600 Busy everywhere to 17 User busy, 500 Server internal error and 503 Service unavailable to 41 Temporary failure, 501 Not implemented to 79 Not implemented, 502 Bad gateway to 38 Network out of order, and 504 Server time-out to 102 Recovery on timer expiry.

Any SIP status code not listed should map to cause code 31, Normal unspecified. The BYE and CANCEL requests, which also tear down a dialog, should usually map to 16, Normal clearing. By default the cause location is encoded so that 6xx codes are given the location user, while 4xx and 5xx codes are given a network location, with the exceptions the memo marks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone network reason for ending a call is matched to a SIP status code, and the match is also given the other way round. A few phone network reasons are left out because they mean something only inside the phone network, such as choosing a different circuit, and those are not translated at all.

sections.title: Telephone Numbers as Tel URIs
sections.content:
SIP proxy servers may route SIP messages on any signalling criteria the network administrators want, but the Request-URI is generally the foremost routing criterion, and the To and From headers are also frequently of interest. SIP to ISUP mapping assumes that proxy servers are interested in at least those three fields, all of which contain URIs, and it frequently requires telephone numbers to be written in them. The most common format for a telephone number in SIP is the tel URL, which may be the whole URI field or may be the user portion of a SIP URI, so a To field may be tel:+17208881000 or sip:+17208881000@level3.com. Whether a gateway or endpoint should use the tel or the SIP format is a matter of local administrative policy: if a host portion would help the surrounding network route the call, the SIP format should be used. A gateway must accept either form from its peers.

The '+' sign before the number in a tel URL says that the digits that follow are a fully qualified E.164 number, meaning a country code comes before any national area or exchange codes. The absence of a '+' may mean the number is only nationally significant, or that a private dialing plan is in use. When a telephone number is the user portion of a URI and there is no '+', the SIP URI should carry the optional ';user=phone' parameter, as in sip:83000@sip.example.net;user=phone.

It is strongly recommended that only internationally significant E.164 numbers be passed between SIP-T gateways, especially when the gateways are in different regions or administrative domains. In most SIP-T networks the gateways are not responsible for end-to-end routing, and a gateway has no way of knowing whether the call will terminate locally or remotely, so it should always assume that an international numbering plan is needed. There is no guarantee that the recipients of the signalling will understand the national dialing plans of the originator, and if the originating gateway does not internationalize the signalling, the context in which the digits were dialled cannot be worked out by the far end.

In ISUP the telephone number appears in a common format used in several parameters, including the Called Party Number and the Calling Party's Number. The memo calls this ISUP format, and the ISUP calling format when it also carries the extra calling party information. The format consists of a byte called the Nature of Address indicator, followed by a byte holding the Numbering Plan Indicator, both prefixed to a variable-length series of bytes holding the digits in Binary Coded Decimal. In the calling party case the Numbering Plan Indicator's byte also holds bit fields for the caller's presentation preferences and the status of any call screening checks done so far. The Numbering Plan Indicator is generally set to the ISDN telephony numbering plan, but that does not mean the digits necessarily contain a country code; the Nature of Address field is what says whether the number is in national or international format, and when it is not, the Nature of Address generally carries information specific to the national dialing plan that can usually be used to convert the number into international format.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number in SIP is written as a tel URL, and a leading plus sign means the number includes its country code. The memo strongly recommends that gateways only pass fully qualified international numbers to each other, because the far end has no way of guessing which country plan a bare number came from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Translating ISUP parameters into SIP headers raises privacy and security concerns beyond those already identified for the other parts of SIP-T. Merely securing the encapsulated ISUP would not be enough for a user who has asked for presentation restriction, if the Calling Party's Number is openly mapped to the From header, and the memo points to the SIP Privacy document for how that function should be handled. Because the scope of the mapping has been restricted to the parameters that are translated into the headers and fields used to route SIP requests, gateways reveal through translation the minimum possible amount of information.

A security analysis of ISUP is beyond the scope of the memo. The risk the memo does identify is that the absence of such an analysis poses a risk if embedded ISUP is interpreted blindly, so gateways should not blindly trust embedded ISUP unless the request was strongly authenticated and the sender is trusted, for example another MGC authorized to use ISUP over SIP in bridge mode. When requests arrive from arbitrary endpoints, gateways should filter any received ISUP, accepting or passing through only known-safe commands and parameters. Filtering by deleting entries believed to be dangerous does not work well.

In most respects the information translated from ISUP to SIP has no special security requirements. It has to be legible to intermediaries in order to be used to route requests, so end-to-end confidentiality would be unnecessary and most likely detrimental, and there are many circumstances in which intermediaries can legitimately overwrite the values, so integrity over these headers is similarly not desirable.

The mapping in the other direction raises more. In the telephone network, policy can stop a user dialling certain invalid or restricted numbers, or selecting certain carrier codes, so gateway operators may want matching policies on the tel URLs and tel URL parameters they accept. The fields used for number portability become tel URL parameters, and users can set them arbitrarily, so an end user could change the end office to which a call is routed, though the memo judges the risk as not grave. Because a SIP user agent can answer an INVITE with any response code, it can dictate, within the boundaries the gateway supports, the cause code the gateway sends in the Release, and operators may want to scrutinise that set of mappings and may wish to implement alternative mappings. A user can also set a To header that differs from the Request-URI, which lets them set the Original Called Number arbitrarily, and that could affect applications relying on it for settlement. The arbitrary population of the From header has well-understood implications for devices that treat it as the identity of the originator, so a gateway that intends to use the From header to fill the calling number in an IAM should authenticate the originator and check that it is allowed to assert that number. Gateways, like all SIP user agents, must support Digest authentication.

Finally, the memo notes the risk in cutting the backwards media path through before the call is answered, because the called user agent could then play arbitrary audio to the caller for an indefinite time. It judges that SIP introduces no risks here that Q.931 to ISUP mapping does not, but says implementers may add an optional timer to cut off early media, and that it is unlikely that more than 20 or 30 seconds of early media is needed to convey status information. A more conservative approach is never to cut backwards media through until a final response has been received, provided the gateway can prevent clipping of the initial media. And because a SIP user agent can launch many simultaneous requests, a gateway may want to restrict the number of simultaneous requests from the same authenticated source.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is careful about embedded signalling: a gateway should not act on ISUP it finds inside a request unless the request was properly authenticated, because the phone network's own security was never analysed here. It also warns that a SIP user agent can choose its own status code, and so can influence the reason for ending the call that reaches the phone network.

messages.label: IAM
messages.note: The call arrives from the phone network as an ISUP setup message.

messages.label: INVITE with ISUP body
messages.note: The ingress gateway puts the ISUP message into the body of the SIP request, which is what gives ISUP transparency.

messages.label: INVITE
messages.note: The request crosses the SIP network, where the voice path between the two media gateways is set up.

messages.label: IAM
messages.note: The egress gateway unwraps the ISUP message and sends it on to the phone network, adjusting it if SIP redirection changed the number.

viz.caption: THE SIP FEATURES THE MAPPING RELIES ON

items.title: Transparent transit
items.text: SIP messages must be able to carry ISUP payloads from gateway to gateway.

items.title: multipart/mixed
items.text: PSTN interworking nodes must understand the multipart/mixed media type.

items.title: Reliable provisional responses
items.text: SIP messages must be sent reliably end to end when interworking with the telephone network.

items.title: Early media
items.text: Playing tones and announcements before the call is answered.

items.title: INFO method
items.text: Carries mid-call events that correspond to no SIP operation.

items.title: Privacy
items.text: A request to hide the caller's number has to be carried across the gateway.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: A CALL FROM SIP INTO THE PHONE NETWORK

messages.label: INVITE
messages.note: The SIP user starts a session. The gateway reserves its media resources here.

messages.label: IAM
messages.note: The gateway maps the request to an ISUP Initial Address Message and starts timer T7.

messages.label: ACM
messages.note: The far exchange says the address is enough to set up the call.

messages.label: 18x
messages.note: The called party status in the ACM is mapped to a provisional SIP response.

messages.label: CPG
messages.note: Call progress, for example that the call is being forwarded.
The gateway sends the final SIP response and establishes the media path.

messages.label: ACK
messages.note: The SIP node acknowledges the final response.
